Dependencies are other packages that are necessary in order for the current package to work
A package defines its dependencies as requirements, roughly a combination of a package name and acceptable versions
The dependencies defined by the current project are called direct dependencies
The dependencies added by each dependency of the current project are called indirect or transitive dependencies
A package you explicitly add to your configuration is treated by uv as a direct dependency
Libraries required by a package you added are indirect or transitive dependencies
During resolution, uv must find a set of package versions that satisfies the project requirements
The resolution must also include the transitive dependencies
Your environment can contain other libraries you never declared directly because transitive dependencies are included
Most packages need other packages to work
Each package declares its dependencies as requirements: a package name plus a range of acceptable versions
When you add a package, uv installs everything that package requires, including requirements of requirements
Direct dependencies are the ones your project defines
Indirect (transitive) dependencies are the ones your direct dependencies bring in
uv looks for one set of package versions that satisfies every requirement at once, including transitive ones
Example: project depends on foo and bar; foo 1.0.0 requires lib>=1.0.0; bar 1.0.0 requires lib>=2.0.0; lib has versions 1.0.0 and 2.0.0
The resolution has to include lib even though it is not listed directly
foo accepts either version of lib, but bar needs 2.0.0 or later, so lib 2.0.0 is picked
Sometimes more than one combination of versions is a valid solution
When multiple solutions are valid, the resolver chooses one valid solution
The dependency specifiers page in the Python Packaging documentation (https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/dependency-specifiers/) describes how requirements are written

uv and pip handle packages that exist on more than one index differently
uv checks indexes in order, with --extra-index-url indexes checked before the default index (PyPI)
uv stops at the first index that contains the package and only considers the versions available there
If the internal index has the package, uv does not consider versions on PyPI, so a version only on PyPI isn't found
pip combines candidate versions from all indexes and picks the best from the combined set
pip doesn't guarantee the order in which it searches indexes
pip assumes packages are unique by name and version across all indexes
uv's default behavior protects against dependency confusion attacks, where a malicious package published on PyPI with an internal package's name gets installed instead
The torchtriton incident in December 2022 is an example (https://pytorch.org/blog/compromised-nightly-dependency/)
If a package exists on the internal index, uv's default is to always install it from there and never from PyPI
The --index-strategy option / UV_INDEX_STRATEGY environment variable has been available since v0.1.29
Index handling can be changed via the --index-strategy command-line option or UV_INDEX_STRATEGY environment variable

unsafe-first-match searches all indexes and prefers the first index that has a compatible version
With unsafe-first-match, if the internal index lacks a compatible version, uv can use the newer release from PyPI
Setting `export UV_INDEX_STRATEGY=unsafe-first-match` or passing `--index-strategy unsafe-first-match` to `uv pip install` enables this behavior
Using unsafe-first-match reintroduces the dependency confusion risk

Publishing to JFrog is supported by adding a publish-url to the index definition
You publish with: uv publish --index private-registry -u "" -p "$JFROG_TOKEN"

Using --token or UV_PUBLISH_TOKEN with JFrog returns a 403 error
uv sends __token__ as the username when --token is used
The workaround is to pass the token as the password
Alternatively, set UV_PUBLISH_USERNAME="" and UV_PUBLISH_PASSWORD="$JFROG_TOKEN"
A full guide for this exists in the uv docs
